title: Kumbhakarna's long sleep
hookLine: a giant opens his mouth to ask for power, and asks for sleep
carry: yoga is for the one who sleeps in measure

cards: Three brothers sit in fierce penance for thousands of years, and the creator Brahma comes to grant each a wish. The gods are terrified of the middle brother.

Kumbhakarna is a giant with an appetite to match, and they fear what he'll ask for. So, in the Ramayana's telling, Brahma calls on Sarasvati, goddess of speech, and she slips onto Kumbhakarna's tongue.
He opens his mouth to ask for his boon, and what comes out is: let me sleep. For years.

teach.h: THE GIANT WHO ASKED FOR SLEEP
teach.b: He gets his wish, and the giant who could have shaken the heavens spends his life asleep. In the popular telling he sleeps six months at a time and wakes for a single day.
When Rama's army reaches Lanka, his brother Ravana needs him, and waking him takes drums, conches, mountains of food and elephants marched over his body. He wakes, he fights bravely, and he falls.
Plenty of Indian families still tease a child who won't get out of bed: get up, Kumbhakarna. Behind the joke is a real teaching.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, paraphrased: yoga isn't for one who eats too much or not at all, nor for one who sleeps too much or stays awake too long.
For the one measured in food and play, in work, in sleep and waking, yoga ends sorrow. Elsewhere he names tamas, the heavy guna, as binding a person through carelessness, laziness and sleep.
So the Hindu teaching isn't that sleep is good or bad. It's measure. Ayurveda says it from the doctor's side.
The Charaka Samhita names three supports, upastambha, that keep a life standing: food, sleep, and brahmacharya, a disciplined way of living.
Happiness and strength, knowing and not knowing, it says, depend on sleep taken rightly or wrongly, in the right measure and at the right time.
So there are two ways to miss: Kumbhakarna's lost years, and the all-nighter. For anyone trading sleep for deadlines, that's the teaching: the night is part of the practice, not time stolen from it.
Sleep trouble that lasts, or exhaustion that won't lift, goes to a doctor.

how: Hindus who follow the Bhagavad Gita treat measured sleep and waking as part of yoga, and Ayurveda's classical routine counts sleep at the right hour among the three supports of life; Kumbhakarna is the household name for anyone who oversleeps.

o: sleep as long as the body wants, since rest is always holy
sleep in measure, not too much or too little, as part of yoga
sleep as little as possible, since only waking hours are spiritual

games.q: the giant and the measure — tap the pairs.
p: asked for sleep instead of power
goddess of speech, on his tongue
yoga for the one measured in it

s: Kumbhakarna meant to ask Brahma for sleep
the gods feared him, and Sarasvati sat on his tongue so his wish came out as sleep.
the Gita says yoga isn't for one who sleeps too much, or too little
Krishna asks for measure in food, play, work, sleep and waking.
in Hindu teaching, the more you sleep, the holier you are
it's measure: the Gita and Charaka both warn against too much and too little.

games.q: it's Saturday. you were up till 4 finishing an essay, and you could sleep till 3pm. what does the Gita's teaching point you to?
o: sleep till 3: the night was short, so even it out.
a measured sleep, then back to a steady hour.
skip sleep: staying awake is the disciplined path.
games.why: Krishna says yoga is for the one measured in sleep and waking. too much and too little both miss: Kumbhakarna on one side, the all-nighter on the other.

practice: Lie down, or sit, and let your weight go into what holds you, a little more with each breath out. Many Hindu households close the day with a short prayer, asking pardon for the day's wrongs before sleep. If you pray, say one now.
If you don't, just name one thing from today you can set down.

wordCard.voice: Sleep. Nidra, in Sanskrit. In the Gita, yoga belongs to the one measured in sleep and waking; for Charaka, sleep is one of life's three supports. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit nidra: sleep. In the Gita (14.8), tamas binds a person through carelessness, laziness and nidra.

carryVoice: Your line: yoga is for the one who sleeps in measure. Not Kumbhakarna's years, not the all-nighter. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 10 (Brahma grants boons to Ravana's brothers; at the gods' request Sarasvati enters Kumbhakarna's mouth and he asks to sleep for many years)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Kumbhakarna woken with drums, conches, food and elephants; he fights and is killed by Rama)
Bhagavad Gita 6.16–17 (yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little; for the one measured in food, recreation, work, sleep and waking, yoga destroys sorrow)
Bhagavad Gita 14.8 (tamas binds through heedlessness, laziness and sleep)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 11.35 (three upastambhas: ahara, svapna, brahmacharya)

Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 21.35–38 (happiness and unhappiness, strength and weakness, knowledge and ignorance, life and death depend on sleep; sleep at the wrong time or in the wrong measure harms)
